tips.title: Added value is price minus bought-in costs
tips.body: **Added** value is what the business **added** to what it **bought in**: selling price minus the cost of the bought-in inputs, and nothing else. Rent and wages were never bought in to make the product, so the moment you subtract them you have slid into profit. Confusing the two is the most common definition slip in 1.1.

tips.title: It takes T-W-O to make a new idea
tips.body: The specification's three reasons new ideas appear spell **T-W-O**: changes in **T**echnology, changes in what consumers **W**ant, and products becoming **O**bsolete. Each one is a door opening: a phone in every pocket, a taste for plant-based food, a DVD player nobody buys any more.

tips.title: Risks and rewards come in three pairs
tips.body: Learn three pairs, not six words. Each risk is a reward turned inside out: business **failure** against business **success**, **financial loss** against **profit**, **lack of security** against **independence**. Given one side in a question, the matching word on the other side is the answer.

tips.title: Risk is what you might lose
tips.body: A **risk** is something that could go wrong for the entrepreneur: losing savings, the business failing. A **reward** is what they gain: profit, independence, a sense of achievement. A regular salary is what an employee gets, so it is neither.

tips.title: Say what the business actually does
tips.body: Every *explain* question wants a chain that ends at **this** business. "It adds value" is generic. "Branding lets the cafe charge £3 rather than £2 for the same coffee, so each sale earns £1 more" is the answer.

tips.title: Do the subtraction before anything else
tips.body: Added value is **selling price minus the bought-in costs**, and nothing else. Write that subtraction down first, then answer whatever the question actually asked. It stops rent, wages and the owner’s time creeping in, which is what turns added value into profit by mistake.

why.matters: Everything you own began with somebody risking their own time and money on an idea nobody had asked for yet. This topic is about why that gamble gets taken, what the person stands to lose and gain, and what a business is actually **for** — which is not making money but meeting a need well enough that people choose to pay. Once you can see **added value**, you can look at any price and ask where it came from, and that question is the start of every business decision in the course.

examples.title: The £3 coffee
examples.body:
Say the beans, milk, cup and lid a café buys in for one latte come to **40p**. Sold at **£3.00**, the added value is **£2.60**: what the café added by turning ingredients into a drink you wanted, in a warm room, in two minutes.

That £2.60 is not the profit. The rent, the barista's wages and the electricity are all paid out of it, and what is left at the end is profit. Two cafés can buy the same beans; the one with the better room and the faster service adds more.

props.caption: one latte: what was bought in, and what it sells for

bars.label: Selling price
bars.note: the gap is £2.60 of added value

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion: the forty pence of bought-in inputs for one latte beside its three pound selling price, the gap being the added value

examples.title: The bake sale
examples.body:
Risk and reward at pocket-money scale. You spend **£12** on flour, eggs and sugar and give up a Saturday to make **30** cupcakes to sell at **£1.50**. If they all go, revenue is £45 and you are **£33** better off: the reward. If it rains and nobody comes, the £12 and the Saturday are gone: the risk.

Notice what you did before you started: checked the weather, asked friends whether they would come. That is a **calculated** risk, and it is the whole of what an entrepreneur does at a larger scale.

props.caption: the risk and the reward of one bake sale

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion comparing the twelve pounds a bake sale could lose against the thirty-three pounds it could gain

examples.title: Three prices for one T-shirt
examples.body:
A plain white T-shirt sells for about **£4**. The same shirt with a printed design might be **£12**, and with a well-known logo on the chest **£30**. The cotton cost almost the same in all three.

The difference is added value from **design** and **branding**: customers pay for how the shirt looks and what it says about them, not for more cotton. Every one of the five ways to add value works like this — the customer pays for something the business put there, and the business gets to keep the gap.

props.caption: roughly the same cotton in all three

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion: a plain T-shirt at four pounds, one with a printed design at twelve, and a branded one at thirty, all made of much the same cotton

steps.title: Why new business ideas appear
steps.body:
Business is **dynamic**: it never sits still, because the world around it does not. The specification gives three reasons new ideas come about.

- **Changes in technology.** Something becomes possible that was not before: smartphones made delivery apps possible, and 3D printing let a one-person workshop make parts to order.
- **Changes in what consumers want.** Customers move towards healthier food, ethical sourcing, convenience, sustainability. A business that notices first serves them first.
- **Products becoming obsolete.** Something is replaced by something better. DVD players went when streaming arrived, and the businesses that made them had to change or close.

And ideas themselves come in two kinds: **original** ideas that did not exist before, and **adapted** ones that take an existing product or service and change it for a new group of customers, which is far more common.

steps.title: Risk and reward
steps.body:
Starting a business means accepting that it might not work. The specification names three of each.

**Risks**

- **Business failure**: the business closes.
- **Financial loss**: the money put in is gone, and for a sole trader their own savings and possessions can go too (topic 1.4 gives this its name: unlimited liability).
- **Lack of security**: no guaranteed income, no sick pay, no paid holiday.

**Rewards**

- **Business success**: something you built that works.
- **Profit**: what is left is yours, with no ceiling on it.
- **Independence**: you decide the product, the hours, the customers.

The two are linked. An employee has security and a fixed salary; an owner gives up both in exchange for the chance of a larger, uncertain return. An entrepreneur does not seek risk, they take **calculated** risks: researched, planned, and worth the possible reward.

check.solution: Lack of security is one of the three risks. The other three are the rewards.

steps.title: What a business is for
steps.body:
The **purpose of business activity** is to produce **goods** (physical things) or **services** (things done for you) that meet customers' **needs**, and in doing so to **add value**.

Added value is the difference between what the inputs cost and what customers will pay:

$$\text{Added value} = \text{selling price} - \text{cost of the bought-in inputs}$$

A chair bought for £40, restored and sold for £95 has £55 of value added. That £55 is **not** the profit: the rent, the wages and the owner's time all come out of it. Only what is left after every other cost is profit.

Adding value is also what lets a business charge more than a rival with the same materials, and there are five ways on the specification to do it.

visuals.alt: A card showing added value as selling price minus the cost of inputs, and profit as revenue minus total costs

check.prompt: A baker buys ingredients for £2 and sells the cake for £11. Calculate the value added.
check.solution: $11 - 2 = £9$. Rent, energy and the baker's time still have to come out of that.

steps.title: Five ways to add value
steps.body:
- **Branding**: a name customers recognise and trust, so they choose it over an unknown rival and pay more.
- **Quality**: it lasts longer, works better or tastes better, so customers return and recommend it.
- **Design**: how it looks and how well it works, which can justify a much higher price for the same materials.
- **Unique selling point (USP)**: something no competitor offers, so there is nowhere else to get it.
- **Convenience**: easier to buy or to use — open later, delivered faster, in the right place.

The test in an exam is always the same: *why would a customer pay more for this than for the cheapest version?* The answer names one of these five.

visuals.alt: Four boxes for branding, quality, design and USP, and convenience around the phrase added value

check.prompt: A corner shop stays open until midnight when every rival closes at six. Which way of adding value is this?
check.solution: Being open when nothing else is makes the shop easier to buy from, which is convenience. Customers pay a little more for it.

markScheme.description: convenience

options: Design
Quality
Branding
Convenience

steps.title: Added value through the whole business
steps.body: Exam questions often chain added value into profit. Work it per item first, then scale it up, then take the fixed costs off. (Fixed costs are the bills that stay the same however many are made — rent, insurance, salaries. Topic 1.3 covers them properly.) Writing those three lines separately keeps the method marks safe.

steps.text: So the £14 pays the rent first, and only £1600 of it is profit

steps.title: What an entrepreneur actually does
steps.body:
An **entrepreneur** is the person who starts and runs a business, and the specification gives them three roles.

1. **Organising resources.** Finding premises, buying stock and equipment, hiring people, arranging finance: turning an idea into something that can trade.
2. **Making business decisions.** What to sell, at what price, to whom, through which channels — and then every decision that follows.
3. **Taking risks.** Putting their own money, and usually their salary and security, behind an idea that might fail.

The third is the one that distinguishes them from an employee, but it is only worth anything alongside the first two: a risk taken without organising or deciding well is just a gamble.

visuals.problem: From idea to trading: what the entrepreneur does at each point

steps.text: Idea: notices that nobody nearby sells repaired bikes
Organises resources: rents a unit, buys tools, arranges a £5000 loan
Decides: which repairs to offer, what to charge, whether to open Sundays
Takes the risk: the £5000 and their salary now depend on customers turning up

check.solution: Gathering what the business needs in order to trade is organising resources. The risk is carried alongside it, but this action is the organising.

steps.title: Your turn: read the case for risk and reward
steps.body:
**Case:** Marcus has worked as a chef for eleven years. He wants to open his own restaurant. He has £22 000 saved, and a bank has offered to lend him a further £40 000. His current job pays a steady salary and he has two young children.

Before the check, list what Marcus stands to lose and what he stands to gain. The case gives you both.

visuals.problem: Underline what the case gives you

A steady salary given up, and two children to support: lack of security
Eleven years of experience: the idea is far from unproven, which lowers the risk
Rewards: all the profit, independence, and a restaurant of his own
steps.note: A good answer names the case facts on both sides, then judges

check.solution: Experience makes the idea more likely to work, which lowers the risk. The loan increases what he owes, the children increase what depends on his income, and the salary is what he would give up.

steps.title: Going deeper: added value is not profit, and risk is not recklessness
steps.body:
Two ideas in this section are worth getting exactly right, because the marks hang on them.

**Added value is not profit.** Added value is price minus the cost of the **bought-in inputs**. Everything else — rent, wages, energy, the owner's own time — still has to come out of it. A shop adding £55 on a chair has not made £55. Examiners see this confused every year.

**Risk is calculated, not sought.** Enterprise means accepting risk that has been researched and judged worth the possible reward. A 12-mark answer that says *entrepreneurs love risk* misses the point; one that says *they take risks they have reason to think will pay* has it.

And for the longer questions: the roles of the entrepreneur are worth arguing about. Risk-bearing is the role nobody else fills, so nothing starts without it — but organising resources and making decisions are what keep the business alive once it has started. Which matters most **depends on the stage**, and naming that is what reaches level 3, the top level.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Business is dynamic.** New ideas come from changes in technology, changes in what consumers want, and products becoming obsolete. Ideas are either **original** or **adapted**.
- **Risks**: business failure, financial loss, lack of security. **Rewards**: business success, profit, independence.
- Entrepreneurs take **calculated** risks, not every risk. Risk can be reduced but never removed.
- **The purpose of business activity** is to produce goods or services that meet customer needs, and to **add value** doing it.
- **Added value** $=$ selling price $-$ cost of the bought-in inputs. It is **not** profit: every other cost comes out of it first.
- **Five ways to add value**: branding, quality, design, a unique selling point, convenience.
- **The entrepreneur's three roles**: organising resources, making business decisions, taking risks.

questions.prompt: A business's product becomes obsolete. What does this mean?

questions.prompt: A craft business buys materials for £6 and sells the finished item for £26. Calculate the value added per item.
questions.solution: Added value $=$ selling price $-$ cost of the inputs $= 26 - 6 = £20$. The £20 pays for the maker's time and skill and, once the other costs are met, becomes profit. It is **not** the profit on its own.

markScheme.description: added value $=$ price $-$ cost of inputs

questions.prompt: A business adds value of £14 on each item and sells 350 items a month. Its fixed costs are £3200 a month. Calculate its profit for the month.
questions.solution: Total value added $= 14 \times 350 = £4900$. That is what is left after the materials, so profit $= 4900 - 3200 = £1700$. Added value covers the fixed costs first; only what remains is profit.

markScheme.description: added value understood as covering fixed costs

questions.prompt: Two friends start a business. One invests savings and works full time in it; the other lends them £2000 at interest and keeps their job. Who carries more risk?
questions.solution: Risk is about what you stand to lose. The working partner has put in capital *and* given up a salary, so failure costs them both. The lender risks only the £2000 and still has a job, and they are paid interest for that risk.

markScheme.description: the one who invested savings and works in it

options: The one who lent £2000, because money lent to a new business is rarely repaid in full
The one who lent £2000, because the interest they earn is taxed as extra income
The one who invested savings and works in it, because both income and capital depend on it
Neither of them, because both have put the same amount of money into the business

questions.prompt: A takeaway is deciding between adding a well-known brand's logo to its packaging under licence, and improving the quality of its ingredients. Analyse which is more likely to add value for this business.
questions.solution: Two chains, both applied. Branding: an established logo means customers recognise and trust it before they taste it, so more of them try it and it can charge more, but a licence fee takes some of that back. Quality: better ingredients cost more per meal, but customers who taste the difference return and recommend it, so repeat custom rises. Level 3 needs both to reach revenue, cost or reputation.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Branding as a way of adding value, applied to a takeaway
Developed to an outcome: recognition brings customers in and supports a higher price, set against the licence fee
Quality as a way of adding value, applied to a takeaway's food
Developed to an outcome: repeat custom and recommendation, set against the higher cost per meal

questions.modelAnswer: Adding a known brand to the packaging adds value through recognition. Customers who have never eaten there already trust the name, which means more of them are willing to try it and to pay a little more than for an unknown takeaway, so revenue per order rises. The licence fee, though, takes a share of every sale, so some of that added value leaves the business. Improving the ingredients adds value through quality. Better food costs more per meal, which raises variable costs, but customers can taste the difference, so they order again and tell others, which builds repeat custom that costs nothing to win. For a takeaway, where most orders come from people nearby who order repeatedly, quality is more likely to add lasting value, because it keeps customers rather than only attracting them once.

questions.prompt: Priya has £8000 of savings and a secure job. She has an idea for a business and must decide whether to leave her job to run it full time, or start it in the evenings while staying employed. Justify which she should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. Full time: all her effort goes in, so the business grows faster and reaches profit sooner, and the reward if it works is larger; but she loses her salary, so both her income and her savings depend on an unproven idea. Evenings: her salary covers her living costs, so failure costs only the savings, but the business grows slowly and a competitor could reach the market first. Judgement: it depends on how proven the idea is and on whether she has anything to fall back on.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice with developed reasons applied to Priya's savings, salary and idea
Developed reasons against the alternative, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: whether the idea is proven, her commitments, or what she can afford to lose

questions.modelAnswer: Priya should start the business in the evenings while keeping her job. Her salary would cover her living costs, so if the idea does not work she loses some of her £8000 but not her income, which means the failure is survivable rather than ruinous. Testing the idea on a small scale also tells her whether customers actually want it before she commits everything to it. Going full time would let her put all her effort in, so the business would grow faster and might reach profit sooner, and the reward would be larger; there is also a risk that a competitor reaches the market first while she works evenings. The deciding factor is that the idea is still unproven. Until she has evidence that customers will pay, the sensible order is to test it cheaply and leave her job once there is real demand, so the reward is pursued without risking everything on a guess.

questions.prompt: A business owner says: "Enterprise means taking every risk you can." Which is the best response?
questions.solution: Entrepreneurship means accepting risk, not seeking it. A market-researched, planned risk with a large possible reward is enterprise; an unnecessary one is carelessness. Risk cannot be removed altogether, which rules out *entrepreneurs avoid risk altogether*.

markScheme.description: calculated risks, weighing reward against loss

options: No: an entrepreneur takes calculated risks, weighing the reward against what could be lost
Yes: the bigger the risk taken, the bigger the reward will be, in every case
No: entrepreneurs avoid risk altogether by planning and researching carefully
Yes: business outcomes are a matter of luck, so the risk taken makes no difference

questions.prompt: Marcus, a chef with eleven years' experience, has opened a restaurant with £22 000 of his own savings and a £40 000 bank loan. Evaluate whether taking risks is the most important of an entrepreneur's roles. Refer to Marcus in your answer.
questions.skill: evaluating the role of the entrepreneur
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then it depends on. For: nobody else will carry the risk, and without someone willing to lose money nothing starts, so risk-taking is what makes the other roles possible. Against: organising resources and making decisions are what turn an idea into a working business, and a risk taken without those is just a gamble; many businesses fail not from too little risk but from poor decisions. Judgement: it depends on the stage, and Marcus, with a loan to repay from month one, is already past the start. At the start, risk-bearing is the role no one else fills; once trading, decision-making and organising resources matter more.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge, applied at least a little, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to this business, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: Taking risks is the role no one else will fill. Marcus has put £22 000 of his own savings behind an idea that might fail, given up a chef's salary, and borrowed £40 000 that he must repay whether or not the restaurant works; without someone willing to do that no new business ever starts, so in that sense risk-bearing makes the other two roles possible. But a risk taken on its own is only a gamble. Organising resources — finding premises, buying stock, hiring the right people — and making decisions about price, product and customers are what turn the idea into something that trades, and most start-ups that fail do so because those decisions were wrong rather than because too little was risked. A person who invests everything in an idea and then manages it badly loses the money just as surely as one who never started. Which role matters most therefore depends on the stage the business is at. At the very beginning, before there is anything to manage, bearing the risk is the role that distinguishes an entrepreneur from everyone else. Once the business is trading, organising resources and making good decisions are what keep it alive, and the original risk has already been taken. For Marcus, with a loan to service from the first month, the decisions about menu prices, staffing and stock are now the role that decides whether the risk he took pays off.

markScheme.description: adapted

questions.prompt: A jeweller buys silver and stones for £14 per necklace and sells each necklace for £45. Calculate the value added per necklace.
questions.solution: Added value $=$ selling price $-$ cost of the bought-in inputs $= 45 - 14 = £31$. The jeweller's time and the rent of the workshop were not bought in to make the necklace, so they are not subtracted here: they come out of the £31 later, on the way to profit.

questions.prompt: An entrepreneur has researched the market, tested the product with 200 customers, and kept her job part-time while the business starts. Which statement best describes her approach to risk?
questions.solution: Research and a part-time job **reduce** the risk: a smaller loss if it fails, and evidence that it might not. They do not **remove** it, because the market can still change and the customers who said yes may not buy. That is a **calculated** risk, which is exactly what enterprise means.

markScheme.description: calculated risk, reduced not removed

options: She has removed the risk of the business failing
She is taking a calculated risk, reduced by research but not removed
She is avoiding risk, so she is not really an entrepreneur
She is taking every risk available to her

examTechnique.body:
Section 1.1 opens Paper 1 and supplies the short definition questions in Section A, plus the framing for case studies about a start-up. The terms have to be exact, because the multiple choice tests the near misses: risk against reward, goods against services, added value against profit.

The marks that decide the grade are on the longer questions about risk and about the entrepreneur's role, and they are lost the same way each year: added value treated as profit, entrepreneurs described as loving risk, and 12-mark answers that pick a role without saying what the answer depends on.
examinerErrors: Calling added value the profit. Added value is price minus the bought-in inputs; rent, wages and the owner's time still come out of it.
Listing a reward as a risk. A regular salary is what an employee has; independence and profit are the rewards an owner gets for giving it up.
Writing that entrepreneurs take every risk. They take calculated risks, researched and judged against the possible reward.
Saying a business can avoid risk altogether. It can be reduced by research and planning, never removed.
Describing the purpose of business as making a profit. The purpose is to meet customer needs by producing goods or services; profit is the result of doing that well.
Naming a way of adding value without saying why a customer would pay more for it. The mark is in the consequence, not the label.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates added value from profit without being asked, and shows the working per item before scaling it up. On risk it quotes the facts in the case on both sides — what the person would lose and what they would gain — and judges with the deciding factor named, such as whether the idea is proven or what they can afford to lose. On the entrepreneur's roles it argues that risk-bearing is the role nobody else fills at the start while organising and deciding matter more once trading, and says the answer depends on the stage.
